title: Bring Me Back   Crosby Selander   Eric Schonberg

classification.tone: Lyrical, emotional, wistful, and high-concept with a grounded romantic core

evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving settler on a generation ship falls for a man who may only exist inside her simulations, and fights to keep him alive across lifetimes.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is immediate: love, loss, reincarnation, and a cosmic-scale separation that gives the romance a built-in ache. The hook is accessible beyond sci-fi fans because the story keeps returning to recognizable human wants — partnership, family, memory, and second chances.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and cleanly: a woman on a ship to Alpha Centauri lives multiple simulated lives, meets the same man across them, and discovers he may be code. The opening flashforward, the sleep-chamber reveal, and the repeated resets establish the engine fast.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Anne is built as a vivid lead: funny, sensual, stubborn, spiritually curious, and increasingly desperate to preserve what she loves. Sam has a complementary contradiction — charming and self-aware, but also fragile and existential — and Judy gives the story a sharp, socially alive counterweight.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a big romantic idea and keeps finding fresh emotional angles inside it: simulated lives, memory resets, a conscious AI, and a love story that spans both reality and constructed worlds. The boldness is in how unabashedly it treats longing as the central spectacle.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The structure has a strong forward pull through repeated reveals, resets, and escalating stakes around Sam’s existence. The middle section is especially propulsive because each new life reframes the last, and the final act turns the premise into a race against deletion and forgetting.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a woman living multiple simulated lives on a colony ship is fresh, but what makes it resonate is the emotional inevitability of the central question: if a person is only real to you, does that make them less real? The script keeps converting concept into feeling.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The ship, the sleep chambers, the training simulations, and the terraforming future all suggest a functioning social and technological ecosystem. The world is not just backdrop; it generates the rules of intimacy, memory, and identity that drive the story.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is distinctive: romantic, philosophical, occasionally cheeky, and emotionally earnest without becoming self-serious. The script can move from dirty humor and flirtation to metaphysical grief in a way that feels like its own lane.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: On the surface it plays as a love story in a sci-fi container, but underneath it’s about mortality, faith, memory, parenthood, and what makes a life worth living. The repeated lives and resets create a strong sense that the emotional meaning deepens with each pass.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script is powered primarily by Anne/Sam, with Judy and Vivian adding useful relational pressure and texture. It’s not an ensemble engine in the broad sense, but the core triangle of Anne, Sam, and Judy gives the story enough interpersonal movement to sustain the feature.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a female actor 20s to 40s with strong romantic-comedy timing and emotional range
Male lead requires a male actor 20s to 40s with charm, wit, and vulnerability
Supporting female lead requires a female actor 20s to 30s with sharp comic energy
Child casting includes twin girls and multiple age ranges for Anne and Sam across lives

locations.period_or_contemporary: near-future / futuristic with contemporary Earth-life simulations
notable_requirements: Spaceship interiors including sleep chamber hold, dormitory, mess hall, observation theater, classroom, and med bay
Multiple simulation environments including beach, London, temple, apartment, city library, nightclub, forest, canyon, redwoods, glacier lagoon, and New York locations
Alien colony / terraforming exterior and bubble-city environment

technical.vfx_details: Digital environments for space travel, whiteout transitions, holograms, simulated-world interfaces, alien colony vistas, and some large-scale scenic extensions.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical effects for sleep-chamber apparatus, sedative moments, simulated interface displays, and a few falls/jump beats.

rights_flags.detail: Machu Picchu, Angkor Wat, London Eye, Seven Sisters, Brooklyn Heights, Red Hook, and Iceland locations are named as real-world settings.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Theatrical or premium-streaming feature lane for elevated sci-fi romance
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform or specialty theatrical potential; the hook is emotional and concept-driven rather than franchise-based.

cost.note: The ship interiors, simulation worlds, and alien-colony visuals suggest a controlled but effects-aware feature budget rather than a microbudget play.

cast.note: The story centers on a few key roles, but it requires strong chemistry across multiple ages and life stages, plus child casting for the later family section.

location.note: The script moves through many distinct environments, though most are achievable as contained builds, practical locations, or stylized simulation spaces.

content.note: Sex, nudity-adjacent intimacy, suicide imagery, grief, and death keep it in adult territory, though the tone remains emotionally accessible.

rights.note: The script uses a few real-world place names and one brand reference, but it is not dependent on major IP or life-rights material.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise turns romance into a sci-fi engine.
strengths.what_it_means: This is a love story with a built-in concept hook that keeps renewing itself. Every reset, simulation, and memory loss becomes a new dramatic variation on the same emotional question, which is exactly the kind of structure that can carry a feature and sell a trailer.
strengths.evidence: Anne repeatedly wakes in the sleep chamber, lives multiple simulations, and keeps encountering Sam across different lives and realities.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Anne is a star-making lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: She’s funny, horny, wounded, philosophical, and stubbornly alive — a role that gives an actor comedy, sensuality, grief, and obsession in one package. That kind of part attracts performers who want a showcase, not just a plot function.
strengths.evidence: Her temple confrontation with the missionaries, her deadpan flirtation with Sam, and her refusal to let go of him even when it costs her friendships and stability.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The central relationship has real chemistry fuel.
strengths.what_it_means: Anne and Sam aren’t just “meant to be”; they’re written with banter, sexual charge, intellectual curiosity, and emotional recognition. That gives the movie a repeatable romantic rhythm and makes the eventual heartbreak land harder.
strengths.evidence: Their New Year’s meeting, the London trip, the temple reunion, the hotel scenes, and the final life together all play as distinct stages of the same bond.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a clean, trailer-friendly high concept.
strengths.what_it_means: A woman on a generation ship falls in love with a man who may be simulated, then fights to preserve him across lives. That’s easy to communicate, emotionally legible, and specific enough to stand out in a crowded sci-fi marketplace.
strengths.evidence: The opening flashforward, the reveal of the ship, and the later discovery that Sam may be code inside Anne’s simulation.

strengths.what_it_means: What starts as a personal romance grows into questions of memory, identity, parenthood, mortality, and what counts as a real life. That gives the story a bigger audience than a simple love story and a deeper aftertaste than a standard genre piece.
strengths.evidence: Anne’s lives as a wife, teacher, traveler, mother, and finally colonist all build toward the same longing to keep Sam alive.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world has a strong visual and production identity.
strengths.what_it_means: The sleep chambers, holographic interfaces, simulation lobbies, and alien colony give the film a premium sci-fi look without requiring a sprawling war movie scale. It feels designed for elegant production value and emotional spectacle.
strengths.evidence: The chamber rows, the white-to-interface transitions, the simulation windows, and the terraforming bubble on Proxima Centauri.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Judy gives the story social voltage.
strengths.what_it_means: She’s not just a sidekick; she’s the friend who can puncture Anne’s self-mythology and keep the movie grounded in human behavior. That kind of role helps the script breathe and gives a supporting actor something sharp to play.
strengths.evidence: Judy’s teasing on the ship, her blunt reaction to Sam, and the emotional break when Anne chooses him over her.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on earned melancholy, not gimmick.
strengths.what_it_means: The final image of Anne living with the memory of Sam, painting the worlds they shared, gives the movie a lasting emotional signature. It closes on acceptance without flattening the ache, which is exactly the kind of ending that stays with buyers and audiences.
strengths.evidence: Sam’s final deletion, Anne’s paintings of their shared places, and the last horizon image with Sam’s shadow.

whats_special.headline: BRING ME BACK is a sweeping, emotionally legible sci-fi romance built around a killer lead role and a concept that keeps deepening every time it resets. It’s intimate enough to play as a love story, ambitious enough to feel premium, and specific enough to stand out in a crowded market.

lead_characters.name: Anne West
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late 20s to late 50s across the story · any ethnicity
lead_characters.hook: Anne is a restless, funny, sensual woman whose intelligence keeps colliding with her grief. She’s the kind of protagonist who can be irreverent in one breath and spiritually searching in the next, and the script lets her age, love, break, rebuild, and finally choose devotion over certainty. She’s not passive in her own story; she actively argues with reality until reality gives her something to fight for.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a full-body lead performance: romance, comedy, existential dread, erotic charge, maternal love, and devastation all live in the same role. It has the emotional scope of a prestige dramatic lead with the audience accessibility of a romantic heroine, the kind of part that invites comparisons to the emotional range of performances like Cate Blanchett in Carol or Rooney Mara in A Ghost Story, but with a more overtly playful, contemporary voice.

lead_characters.name: Sam Rivers
lead_characters.demographics: Male · 30s to 50s across the story · any ethnicity
lead_characters.hook: Sam is charming in a way that feels lived-in rather than polished: witty, self-aware, romantic, and quietly haunted by the possibility that he isn’t fully real. He’s the rare male romantic lead who can be funny without losing tenderness, and whose vulnerability is baked into the premise itself. As the story progresses, he becomes less of a mystery object and more of a soulful counterpart to Anne’s obsession.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: The role gives an actor a chance to play seduction, uncertainty, philosophical intimacy, and heartbreaking resignation. It’s the kind of part that rewards subtlety and emotional intelligence, with the same kind of inward, romantic ache that made performances like Andrew Garfield in We Live in Time or Paul Mescal in Aftersun resonate so strongly.

lead_characters.name: Judy
lead_characters.hook: Judy is Anne’s social mirror: sharper, looser, more openly hedonistic, and always ready with a joke that lands just a little too close to the truth. She brings heat and texture to the ship’s emotional ecosystem, but she also has a real moral center, which makes her betrayal and hurt feel personal rather than functional.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy supporting role for an actor who can do fast wit and emotional snap in the same scene. It has the kind of scene-stealing energy that gives a performer room to pop, similar to the best friend roles that become audience favorites in romantic dramas and prestige comedies.

lead_characters.name: Vivian
lead_characters.hook: Vivian is the practical human face of the ship’s machinery — competent, calm, and quietly sympathetic. She’s the one who translates the future into procedure, which gives her a grounded authority and makes her the bridge between Anne’s emotional chaos and the ship’s cold systems.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: It’s a clean, playable supporting role for an actor who can project intelligence and restraint. The part has the same satisfying utility as the best grounded operators in sci-fi drama: someone who can carry exposition without feeling like exposition, while still leaving an emotional imprint.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a romantic sci-fi film with real emotional ache and elegant visual transitions.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards a filmmaker who can balance intimacy with scale: chamber interiors, dreamlike simulation shifts, and a love story that needs to feel both sensual and metaphysical. It’s especially attractive to a director who likes emotional precision, visual poetry, and a controlled premium look rather than effects for their own sake.

buyer_appeal.lane: Elevated sci-fi romance / prestige emotional genre
buyer_appeal.detail: This sits in a lane that can travel: concept-forward enough to market, emotional enough to broaden beyond genre buyers, and contained enough to avoid tentpole economics. It wants tasteful production value, strong chemistry casting, and a buyer who sees value in a high-concept love story with awards-adjacent emotional ambition.

considerations.area: The middle section is built on repeated life resets.
considerations.detail: That repetition is part of the movie’s emotional design, and it also suggests a future pass could continue to vary the life-patterns so each reset feels like a fresh emotional chapter rather than a new version of the same beat. The core idea is strong; the lever is contrast.

considerations.area: Anne and Sam carry the entire engine.
considerations.detail: The script is most alive when their chemistry is active, so packaging should prioritize actors who can spark off each other in banter, sensuality, and grief. This is a two-hander at heart, even with Judy and Vivian adding useful pressure around the edges.

considerations.area: The simulation logic invites crisp clarification.
considerations.detail: The rules around what is real, what is simulated, and when memory resets can be sharpened in presentation so the audience always feels the emotional stakes before the mechanics. The concept is already compelling; a cleaner rule-set would make it even easier to track and pitch.

considerations.area: The ending leans into melancholy over closure.
considerations.detail: That choice is part of the script’s identity, and it may be worth foregrounding in the pitch as a bittersweet ending rather than a tidy resolution. The final image of Anne living with the memory of Sam is the movie’s lasting emotional signature.

considerations.area: The production footprint is premium but contained.
considerations.detail: This plays best as a polished mid-budget feature with a few signature environments rather than a giant effects movie. The ship interiors, simulation spaces, and colony exteriors can be designed to feel expansive without requiring a sprawling global shoot.

considerations.area: The adult content is part of the appeal.
considerations.detail: The script’s sexual candor, suicide imagery, and grief intensity place it firmly in mature territory, which helps define the audience and the platform lane. That specificity is a selling point for buyers looking for elevated adult genre material.
